title: The Shut Door and the Olive Leaf: the Ark, the Two Mountains, and the Nine Hundred and Fifty Years
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Kufa plain, Lamech names his son Rest
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the year is Ussher's flood date of 2349 BC counted back six hundred years, and Genesis names no birthplace
stops.campa: On the plain between the two rivers, in the tenth generation from Adam, Lamech at a hundred and eighty-two years fathers a son and calls him Noah, which is to say rest. The ground has lain under a curse since the garden, and men break their hands on it. Lamech says over the cradle that this one will bring relief from the work and from the toil of the hands, and the saying stands as the whole of the child's inheritance. He grows in a world already old, among fathers who count their years by centuries and a soil that gives grudgingly.
stops.quote: this one shall bring us relief from our work and from the toil of our hands
stops.quote_source: Genesis 5:29, New Revised Standard Version Updated Edition
suggested_refs: The Genesis 5 genealogy of the ten antediluvian patriarchs, from Adam to Noah
sources: James Ussher, Annals of the World (1650), via the Ussher chronology

stops.name: Kufa plain, the hundred and twenty years
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; the 120 years are Rashi's eleventh-century reading of Genesis 6:3, and the age of 480 follows from it
stops.campa: The earth fills with violence in every quarter, and a term is set to the patience of heaven: his days shall be a hundred and twenty years. The rabbis read the sentence as a stay of execution rather than a lifespan, a century and a score granted so that the generation may turn and be spared. Noah is near four hundred and eighty. He begins to cut timber where his neighbours can watch him cut it, and the felling of each tree is a sermon that nobody in the country answers.
suggested_refs: Rashi's commentary on Genesis 6:3, reading the 120 years as a grace period for repentance

stops.name: Kufa plain, the sons of the five hundredth year
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Genesis 5:32 gives an age and not a year, and Jubilees dates the three births separately
stops.campa: At five hundred years Noah begets Shem, Ham, and Japheth, three sons for a world that will need repeopling out of a single tent. Genesis sets all three births in one breath of the genealogy. The Book of Jubilees, written in the Second Temple period, dates each birth on its own and gives Noah a named wife, Emzara daughter of Rakeel, married in the twenty-fifth jubilee. Between the two accounts the household is the same household: eight people who will shortly be the whole of humankind.
suggested_refs: Book of Jubilees 4:33 in the R. H. Charles translation, naming Emzara daughter of Rakeel
sources: Book of Jubilees 4:33 (R. H. Charles translation)

stops.name: Kufa plain, the measure of the ark
stops.date_confidence: undated in Genesis; placed between the birth of the sons and the flood
stops.campa: The word comes with dimensions attached: gopher wood, rooms within, pitch inside and out, three hundred cubits by fifty by thirty, a door set in the side. Three decks, no rudder, no mast, no sail. It is not a ship for sailing but a chest for keeping, built to be shut and to float where it is driven. Noah is a just man, perfect in his generations, and he walks with God; he lays down a hull longer than any vessel the next four thousand years will launch, on dry ground, a long way from any sea.
stops.quote: Make thee an ark of gopher wood; rooms shalt thou make in the ark, and shalt pitch it within and without with pitch. And this is the fashion which thou shalt make it of: The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits.
suggested_refs: The cubit specifications of Genesis 6:14-16, source of every later ark reconstruction

stops.name: Kufa plain, the beasts two by two and seven by seven
stops.date_confidence: undated; the two animal counts stand in the same narrative and are not reconciled by it
stops.campa: Two of every living thing, male and female, are to come to him and be kept alive: so runs the command. Then the command is given again with a different arithmetic, seven pairs of every clean beast and of every fowl of the air and one pair of the unclean, and the two orders stand side by side in the one book without being reconciled. The animals come to the door of themselves, cattle and creeping things and every fowl after his kind, and Noah does according to all that God commands him, whichever tally the beasts obey.
stops.quote: Behold, I, even I, do bring a flood of waters upon the earth, to destroy all flesh, wherein is the breath of life, from under heaven; and every thing that is in the earth shall die.
suggested_refs: The doubled animal instructions of Genesis 6:19-20 and 7:2-3, read by scholars as Priestly and Yahwist material combined

stops.name: Kufa, the timbers on the site of the mosque
stops.date_confidence: traditional site; the Kufa shipyard is post-Quranic exegesis, carried in Shia tradition and recorded by al-Masudi in the tenth century
stops.campa: Islamic memory sets the shipyard here, on the ground that will one day carry the Great Mosque of Kufa, and the tenth-century historian al-Masudi has the finished hull begin its voyage from this place. Noah works the timber for a hundred years and more within sight of the people he is building against; they pass, and look, and go home. Josephus, writing for Rome, gives the vessel four stories where Genesis gives three. The count of decks changes with the teller. The door in the side does not.
stops.quote: That he should make an ark of four stories high, three hundred cubits long, fifty cubits broad, and thirty cubits high.
stops.quote_source: Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book I, ch. 3 (William Whiston translation)
suggested_refs: The Great Mosque of Kufa, held in Shia tradition to stand on the ground where the ark was built
sources: Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews I.3 (Whiston)

segments.name: The Fountains of the Great Deep

stops.name: Kufa, the oven gushes water
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text; Genesis 7:11 dates the day, while the Kufa location of the oven is later exegesis
stops.campa: The sign, when it comes, is domestic and absurd: water rises out of a bread oven. The Quran marks the flood's beginning at the gushing of the tannur, and the commentators place that oven at Kufa, in Noah's own house, on the ground of the later mosque. There is no thunder in the sign and no crack of the sky. A baking oven fills and runs over, and by that small mouth the deep announces itself. Noah loads at once, taking of every kind two, and his household with them.
stops.quote: until, when Our command came, and the oven gushed forth (with water)
suggested_refs: The tannur of Quran 11:40, sited by exegetical tradition within the Great Mosque of Kufa

stops.name: Kufa, eight souls go aboard
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 7:13); the absolute year follows the Ussher reckoning
stops.campa: Eight souls go up the ramp: Noah, his wife, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and the three wives of his sons. Behind them the beasts are already stalled by their kinds, the clean and the unclean lodged apart, food gathered for all of them. The command that opens the door is a summons and not an escape. On the seventeenth day of the second month of the six hundredth year of his life the door is shut, and it is shut from the outside, and it will not be opened again for three hundred and seventy days.
stops.quote: And the Lord said unto Noah, Come thou and all thy house into the ark; for thee have I seen righteous before me in this generation.
suggested_refs: Genesis 7:13-16, the roll of the eight who enter the ark on the day the rain begins

stops.name: Kufa, the windows of heaven open
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 7:11-12); a solar month numbering is imposed here on a lunar reckoning
stops.campa: The same day the two waters that were divided at the creation come back together. Below, the fountains of the great deep burst open; above, the windows of the heavens are opened, and the rain falls forty days and forty nights on a plain that has never seen a river leave its bed. The world is unmade in the order in which it was made, the firmament first. Nothing in the account describes the noise. The ark lifts off its blocks and is carried, and the country of Noah's whole life goes under behind it.
stops.quote: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on that day all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the windows of the heavens were opened.
stops.quote_source: Genesis 7:11, New Revised Standard Version Updated Edition
suggested_refs: Genesis 7:11-12, the undoing of the second day of creation

stops.name: Greater Ararat, fifteen cubits above the summits
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 7:17-20); the month is assigned within the hundred and fifty days
stops.campa: The waters increase and bear the ark up, and it goes upon the face of them. Fifteen cubits above the highest summit under the whole heaven the flood prevails, and the last peak of the world closes over. The vessel has no steering and needs none, for there is nothing left to steer between. A hundred and fifty days the water keeps its height. Somewhere beneath the hull, fathoms down and four hundred miles from the shipyard, stands the mountain the ark will ground on when the level falls.
suggested_refs: Genesis 7:17-20, the fifteen cubits above the covered mountains

stops.name: The drowned plain, all flesh blotted out
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 7:21-23); the month is assigned within the hundred and fifty days
stops.campa: Every living substance is destroyed from off the face of the ground: man and cattle, the creeping things, the fowl of the heaven, all in whose nostrils is the breath of life. The cities of the plain between the rivers lie under fathoms. The fields Lamech cursed, and that his son was named to relieve, are silt. Only Noah remains alive, and they that are with him in the ark. The relief the name promised is delivered exactly as the name promised it, by the removal of everyone whose hands were toiling.
suggested_refs: Genesis 7:21-23, the blotting out of every living thing on the face of the earth

stops.name: Mecca, the ark circles the House
stops.date_confidence: legend; the Mecca detour is al-Masudi's, absent from both Quran and Genesis, and not the dominant Islamic account
stops.campa: One strand of Islamic tradition carries the ark south before it turns north. Al-Masudi has the vessel sail from Kufa to Mecca and circle the House there before making for the resting mountain, so that the hull passes over the sanctuary while the sanctuary is drowned. Abraham will raise the foundations of that House with Ishmael long after the water has drained, descended through Shem, who is aboard this ship now. The stone the ark circles and the stone Abraham sets are the same stone, once submerged and once dry.
suggested_refs: Al-Masudi's account of the ark's voyage from Kufa by way of Mecca to Mount Judi

stops.name: The open water, God remembers Noah
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:1-3); the hundred and fifty days counted from the second month, seventeenth day
stops.campa: The hundred and fifty days end. God remembers Noah, and every living thing, and all the cattle that are with him in the ark, and makes a wind to pass over the earth, the same wind that moved on the face of the waters before there was any land at all. The fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven are stopped, the rain is restrained, and the water goes down continually. Inside the hull nobody can see it happen. The first evidence the household receives is a shudder along the keel.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:1, the wind sent over the water, echoing the spirit moving on the face of the deep

stops.name: Mountains of Ararat, the ark comes to rest
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:4); the single peak, as against the region, is an eleventh-century identification
stops.campa: In the seventh month, on the seventeenth day, the keel takes ground. Five months to the day since the door was shut, the ark stops moving and stays where it has stopped. The text names a region and not a peak: the mountains of Ararat, the highland the Assyrians called Urartu. The white cone that carries the name today is an identification Armenians will make in the eleventh century and Europe will learn from a travelling friar two hundred years after that. Under the hull, for the first time in five months, there is something solid.
stops.quote: And the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, upon the mountains of Ararat.
suggested_refs: The Urartu highland of Assyrian record, the region Genesis 8:4 actually names

stops.name: Mount Judi, the other landing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the Quran (11:44); the coordinate is the traditional Cudi Dagi, and the Judi and Ararat traditions conflict outright
stops.campa: Two hundred miles south-west of the white cone, another mountain holds the same claim and holds it earlier. The Quran names al-Judi, and the Syriac churches of Mesopotamia named it before the Quran did, a long ridge above the Tigris where the ark is said to settle and where pilgrims keep a shrine. Each tradition keeps its own mountain, and no text harmonises them. The command that ends the flood is spoken to the ground and to the sky rather than to Noah: swallow your water, withhold your rain.
stops.quote: And it was said, 'O earth! Swallow up your water. And O sky! Withhold your rain.' The floodwater receded and the decree was carried out. The Ark rested on Mount Judi, and it was said, 'Away with the wrongdoing people!'
stops.quote_source: Quran 11:44, translation by Mustafa Khattab, The Clear Quran
suggested_refs: Cudi Dagi above the Tigris in Sirnak province, the Quranic and Syriac landing place

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the tops of the mountains appear
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:5)
stops.campa: The water goes down continually until the tenth month, and on the first day of the tenth month the tops of the mountains are seen. Noah has been aboard eight months. The ridges come up black out of the falling water, one after another, in the reverse of the order in which they went under, and the household counts them from the one window. Nothing yet is dry. What is visible is rock without soil on it and without a green thing, and the covering of the ark stays fastened while the world reappears.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:5, the mountain tops seen on the first day of the tenth month

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the raven
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:6-7); reckoned forty days after the tenth month, first day, so still in the six hundredth year
stops.campa: Forty days after the summits show, Noah opens the window he has made and puts out a raven. It goes forth to and fro until the waters are dried up from off the earth, and it does not come back to the hand that released it. A carrion bird over a drowned world does not lack for landing. Later readers will hear a reproach in the raven and set it against the dove that follows; the verse itself records only the flight, out and back and out again over water, the first free movement of any creature since the door was shut.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:6-7, the raven that goes to and fro and does not return

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the first dove
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:8-9)
stops.campa: Then he sends a dove from his hand, to see if the waters are abated from off the face of the ground. She finds no rest for the sole of her foot and returns to the ark, and Noah puts forth his hand and takes her and pulls her in to him. It is the one place in the account where the text gives him a gesture instead of an obedience. Everything the household knows of the state of the world it now learns from the feet of a bird: water still, from the mountain out to wherever her wings gave out.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:8-9, the dove taken back in by hand

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the olive leaf
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:10-11)
stops.campa: Seven days he waits, and sends her out again. She comes in to him in the evening, and in her mouth is an olive leaf plucked off, green, torn from a tree that stood under the flood and lived. So Noah knows the waters are abated from off the earth. The proof that the world is habitable is not the mountain under the keel but a leaf small enough to carry in a beak, torn off somewhere the household cannot see. Not only rock has come back. Growing wood has come back, and something is alive down there besides the eight of them.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:10-11, the olive leaf pluckt off, brought in at evening

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the dove that does not return
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:12)
stops.campa: He stays yet another seven days and sends the dove forth a third time, and she does not return to him any more. The bird has found ground she prefers to the ship, which is the last message she is able to send. Noah now has the whole answer his three soundings can give him. Still he does not open the ark. He waits out the turn of the year with the covering fastened, a man of six hundred years keeping the discipline of the shut door until the word that shut it says otherwise.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:12, the third dove, which returned not again unto him any more

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the covering removed
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:13), which dates it to the first day of the first month of the six hundred and first year
stops.campa: On the first day of the first month of the six hundred and first year of his life, Noah removes the covering of the ark and looks, and the face of the ground is dry. It is a new year in a country with no landmarks left: no boundary stone, no field, no house, no smoke anywhere on the horizon. Light comes into the hull for the first time since the second month of the year before. Even so he does not go out. Fifty-seven days more the household stays aboard a grounded ship on dry land, waiting to be told.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:13, the removal of the covering in the six hundred and first year

stops.name: Greater Ararat, the dry earth and the going forth
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:14-19)
stops.campa: In the second month, on the seven and twentieth day, the earth is dried, and the word comes: go forth of the ark, thou and thy wife and thy sons and thy sons' wives with thee, and bring forth every living thing that is with thee, that they may breed abundantly in the earth. The door opens outward on a world with one family in it. The animals go out by their kinds and the wild ones go unherded, and the ark is left empty where it grounded, high on the mountain, above the line where anything grows.
suggested_refs: Genesis 8:14-19, the command to go forth and breed abundantly

stops.name: Mount Lubar, the altar of every clean beast
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 8:20); the coordinate follows the Ararat identification, and Jubilees names the altar mountain Lubar, which nobody has since located
stops.campa: The first act on dry ground is a killing. Noah builds an altar and takes of every clean beast and of every clean fowl, which is what the seven pairs were counted for, and offers them burnt. The Book of Jubilees names the mountain of that altar Lubar, one of the mountains of Ararat, a peak no later traveller has been able to point to. The smoke goes up off a world with no other fire on it, and Josephus says the prayer that goes up with it asks that nature might hereafter keep its former orderly course.
stops.quote: And Noah builded an altar unto the Lord; and took of every clean beast, and of every clean fowl, and offered burnt offerings on the altar. And the Lord smelled a sweet savour; and the Lord said in his heart, I will not again curse the ground any more for man's sake.
suggested_refs: Mount Lubar of Jubilees 5:28 and 7:1, the unlocated peak of the first altar

stops.name: Foot of Ararat, the blessing and the blood
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 9:1-7); the day is assigned after the disembarkation
stops.campa: The blessing of the first creation is spoken a second time, over eight people: be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth. What is new in it is the fear. Every beast of the earth and fowl of the air is delivered into the hand of man, and every moving thing that lives is meat now, save that the blood is forbidden, for the blood is the life. And whoso sheds man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed, for in the image of God made he man. The world restarts with a rule against the thing that filled it before.
stops.quote: And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said unto them, Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth.
suggested_refs: Genesis 9:1-7, the Noachide grant of meat and the prohibition of blood

stops.name: Foot of Ararat, the bow set in the cloud
stops.date_confidence: attested to the text (Genesis 9:8-17); the day is assigned after the disembarkation
stops.campa: God establishes his covenant with Noah, with his seed after him, and with every living creature of the earth, and binds himself by it: never again shall all flesh be cut off by the waters of a flood, never again shall a flood destroy the earth. The token is hung where both parties can see it. A bow set in the cloud is a weapon laid down, drawn and left unstrung against the sky, and the text says it is put there as a reminder to God rather than to men, so that he shall look upon it and remember.
stops.quote: I do set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between me and the earth.
suggested_refs: Genesis 9:8-17, the covenant with every living creature and the sign of the bow

stops.name: Akhuri, the first vineyard
stops.date_confidence: undated in Genesis; the Akhuri site is Armenian local tradition and the year is a placement after the descent
stops.campa: Noah becomes a husbandman and plants a vineyard, the first vine in the world after the water. Armenian tradition puts the planting on the north-eastern slope of the mountain, at the village of Akhuri, whose name the travellers gloss as he planted the vine, and the vines there were shown to visitors as Noah's own stock into the nineteenth century. A man of six hundred and some years, who has outlived the whole generation of the earth, sets cuttings into the mud of a mountain and waits for them to take.
suggested_refs: The vines of Akhuri, modern Yenidogan in Aralik district, held to descend from Noah's planting
sources: Friedrich Parrot's etymology of Arghuri from the Armenian for he planted the vine

stops.name: Akhuri, the tent and the uncovering
stops.date_confidence: undated in Genesis; the coordinate is carried over from the Armenian vineyard tradition, which Genesis does not support
stops.campa: He drinks of the wine and is drunken, and lies uncovered within his tent. There is no precedent for what the drink will do to him; the fruit is new and so is the fermentation, and the Church Father John Chrysostom will excuse him on exactly that ground, the first man in the world to taste wine and nobody to warn him. Ham, the father of Canaan, sees the nakedness of his father and tells his two brethren outside. Shem and Japheth take a garment on both their shoulders, walk backward, and cover him with their faces turned away.
suggested_refs: John Chrysostom's defence of Noah as the first human being to taste wine

stops.name: Akhuri, the curse laid on Canaan
stops.date_confidence: undated in Genesis; the coordinate is the vineyard tradition's, not the text's
stops.campa: Noah awakes from his wine and knows what his younger son has done to him, and the curse he speaks falls not on Ham but on Ham's son. Cursed be Canaan, a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren. Blessed be the Lord God of Shem, and God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem. The map of the nations is laid down in three sentences spoken by an old man on the morning after, and the peoples of the earth will be sorted, conquered and enslaved by them for four thousand years.
stops.quote: Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren. And he said, Blessed be the Lord God of Shem; and Canaan shall be his servant.
suggested_refs: Genesis 9:24-27, the curse of Canaan and the blessing of Shem and Japheth

stops.name: The Mesopotamian plain, the seventy nations
stops.date_confidence: undated; Genesis 10 is a genealogy without years, and the count of seventy is the traditional tally of its names
stops.campa: By the sons of Noah the nations are divided in the earth after the flood, and Genesis counts them out: the sons of Japheth to the isles of the Gentiles, the sons of Ham to Egypt and Canaan and to Nimrod's cities in Shinar, the sons of Shem eastward toward the mountain. Seventy peoples, every one traced back to three men who walked down off a mountain, every tongue and family and coastline of the known world hung on a single household. The plain that drowned fills again from the north with the children of the eight.
suggested_refs: The Table of Nations of Genesis 10, seventy peoples from three sons

stops.name: Nakhchivan, the place of first descent
stops.date_confidence: undated; Armenian local tradition, with Josephus attesting a Place of Descent shown to visitors in the first century
stops.campa: South-east of the mountain, on the Araxes, a city keeps the memory in its name. Armenian tradition reads Nakhchivan as the place of first descent, the ground where Noah comes down off the highland and settles his household, and Josephus records that the Armenians of his own day call the site the Place of Descent and show the remains of the ark to travellers there. The man born on a plain between two rivers ends his life in the mountains, within a day's ride of the water line.
stops.quote: the Armenians call this place ... The Place of Descent; for the ark being saved in that place, its remains are shown there by the inhabitants to this day.
stops.quote_source: Flavius Josephus, Antiquities of the Jews, Book I, ch. 3 (William Whiston translation)
suggested_refs: Nakhchivan on the Araxes, whose name Armenian tradition glosses as the place of descent

stops.name: Cizre, the second city under Judi
stops.date_confidence: undated; the tradition is recorded by the geographer al-Harawi, who died in 1215, and rests entirely on the Judi identification
stops.campa: Below Judi, on the Tigris, a second city claims him. The medieval geographers of Islam, al-Harawi among them, record Jazirat ibn Umar, now Cizre, as the second town Noah founds after the flood, its claim resting wholly on the mountain above it being the true landing place. Nakhchivan and Cizre cannot both be right, and each stands at the foot of a different mountain, so that the argument over where the ark grounded is also an argument over which town is the oldest in the world.
suggested_refs: Al-Harawi's Ziyarat, recording Jazirat ibn Umar as Noah's second city

stops.name: Nakhchivan, the nine hundred and fiftieth year
stops.date_confidence: traditional; Genesis 9:29 gives the age of 950 and the absolute year follows the Ussher reckoning, while no burial place is given anywhere in the text
stops.campa: Noah lives after the flood three hundred and fifty years, and all his days are nine hundred and fifty years, and he dies. He is the last of the long-lived fathers, and nobody born after him will reach half his count. Genesis records the total and gives no grave, and into that silence three shrines are built: a mausoleum at Nakhchivan, a stone chamber in the Lebanese valley of the Bekaa, and the ground at Cizre. The Quran gives the same nine hundred and fifty years to the preaching he did before the water came.
stops.quote_source: Quran 29:14, on the years Nuh spent among his people, cited via the Wikipedia article 'Noah in Islam'
suggested_refs: The rebuilt mausoleum of Noah in the old city of Nakhchivan, photographed in 1902 before its reconstruction

segments.name: The Older Flood and the Rival Graves

stops.name: Nineveh, the flood on the eleventh tablet
stops.date_confidence: the tablet survives in Ashurbanipal's seventh-century library; the epic reached something like its known form c. 1300-1000 BCE on older Sumerian flood material
stops.campa: In the library of the Assyrian kings at Nineveh, on the eleventh tablet of the epic of Gilgamesh, another man is warned by a god, builds a vessel, seals it with pitch, loads his household and the beasts, rides out a flood that drowns mankind, grounds on a mountain, and sends out birds to test the water. His name is Utnapishtim, and the Sumerian tradition behind him, the Ziusudra material, is older than the tablet. Scholars will argue for a century and a half over which telling came first, and will not settle it.
suggested_refs: Tablet XI of the Standard Babylonian Gilgamesh, from the library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh
sources: Wikipedia, 'Genesis flood narrative', summarising comparative Assyriology

stops.name: Mount Ararat, the mountain takes the name
stops.date_confidence: eleventh century for the Armenian identification; 1254 is William of Rubruck's return from the Mongol court, by which Europe learned it
stops.campa: The mountain that carries the name today did not always carry it. Armenians identify the peak above the Araxes as the resting place from about the eleventh century, reasoning that the highest ground would be first to surface as the water fell, and the Franciscan William of Rubruck, riding home from the Mongol court, writes the identification into Europe. The Syriac churches had said Judi. Genesis said a region. From here on Christendom says Ararat, and the case is closed by repetition rather than by evidence.
suggested_refs: William of Rubruck's Itinerarium, reporting the Armenian identification of Ararat to Latin Europe
sources: William of Rubruck, thirteenth-century travel account

stops.name: Karak Nuh, the forty-metre grave
stops.date_confidence: the shrine's inscriptions are fourteenth-century; the beginning of the tradition itself is undated
stops.campa: In the Bekaa valley, at Karak Nuh above Zahle, a stone chamber holds a grave more than thirty metres long, venerated since the Middle Ages as the tomb of Noah, kept chiefly by Shia Muslims though Melkites and Maronites come to it too. Fourteenth-century inscriptions are cut inside the chamber. Scholars who measure the masonry answer that it is a surviving span of a Roman aqueduct, and the two readings lie on top of one another without touching: a buried giant, or a length of engineering built to carry water.
suggested_refs: The long stone chamber at Karak Nuh, Zahle, with its fourteenth-century inscriptions

stops.name: Rome, Arca Noe plank by plank
stops.date_confidence: attested (imprint date)
stops.campa: In Rome the Jesuit Athanasius Kircher publishes Arca Noe and builds the ship again on paper, plank by plank. He works out the stalls by species and the fodder each will eat across a year, the water casks, the drainage, the arrangement of the three decks, and engraves the whole in cutaway so that a reader can walk it. The problem he has set himself is arithmetic: whether the cubits given in Genesis can hold the creatures given in Genesis. He concludes that they can, and prints plans that will be copied for two centuries.
suggested_refs: The cutaway engravings of the ark's three decks in Kircher's Arca Noe, Amsterdam 1675

stops.name: Rome, the nations descend from the sons
stops.date_confidence: attested (imprint date)
stops.campa: Four years later Kircher publishes Turris Babel and follows the other half of the story out of the ark. The confusion of tongues at the tower is the hinge and the descent of every nation from the sons of Noah is the engine: Japheth to Europe, Ham to Africa, Shem to Asia, each language and each people run back along a genealogical line to one of three men who walked down a mountain. A universal history of the human race is built out of a single chapter of Genesis and a household of eight survivors.
suggested_refs: Kircher's Turris Babel (1679), tracing every nation and tongue to the sons of Noah

stops.name: Scotland, the sons at their father's grave
stops.date_confidence: attested for the manuscript's date of 1726; its place of writing is disputed and the coordinate is provisional
stops.campa: A manuscript copied in 1726 tells how the sons of Noah go to their father's grave to seek a secret he had held in life, and how, the body having failed them, they raise it by grip and by word and take what is left to take. The manuscript names Noah and nobody else. Later readers of the craft will find in that scene the ancestor of the raising of Hiram Abiff, the murdered builder of the Temple, lifted out of his grave by the same means. The equation belongs to the readers and not to the manuscript.
suggested_refs: The Graham Manuscript of 1726 and its account of the sons raising Noah by grip and by word

stops.name: Akhuri, the monastery under the snow line
stops.date_confidence: attested; Parrot reached the summit on 9 October 1829
stops.campa: The monastery of Saint Hakob stands on the north-eastern slope at some nineteen hundred metres, beside the village of Akhuri and the vines, eight centuries old and holding the mountain's Christian claim. In October 1829 the Dorpat physician Friedrich Parrot makes it his base camp and completes the first recorded ascent to the summit, and finds on the ice nothing but ice. The climb settles nothing about the ark and a great deal about the mountain: it can be gone up, and from now on men will keep going up it.
suggested_refs: The monastery of Saint Hakob at 1,943 metres, base camp of the 1829 first ascent

stops.name: Akhuri, the mountain falls on the village
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: On the twentieth of June 1840 an earthquake shakes the mountain and brings the slope down. The village of Akhuri, the monastery of Saint Hakob, the vineyard the tradition pointed to and a Kurdish encampment above it are buried in a single afternoon, and nothing is rebuilt on the site. The oldest Christian institution on Ararat is destroyed by Ararat. The vines said to descend from Noah's own planting go with the village that showed them, and the mountain is left holding the name and the story alone.
suggested_refs: James Bryce's account of the 1840 landslide that took the village, the monastery and the encampment

stops.name: Mount Ararat, two hundred sightings
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1856 start of the sighting claims; the tally of about two hundred is cumulative to the present day
stops.campa: From 1856 onward the mountain is climbed by people looking for one thing. Some two hundred claimants out of more than twenty countries report sighting the ark on Ararat: in a glacier, in a crevasse, from an aeroplane, under snow that melted the one year and never melted again. No expedition brings down a plank, a nail, or a photograph that survives inspection. The claims accumulate for a century and a half and yield no object at all, and each new party climbs past the ground the last one searched.
suggested_refs: The catalogue of ark sighting claims on Ararat since 1856, classed by scholarship as pseudoarchaeology

stops.name: Durupinar, the boat shape in the mud
stops.date_confidence: attested; exposure on 19 May 1948, aerial identification in October 1959
stops.campa: Heavy rain and earthquakes on the nineteenth of May 1948 strip the soil off a ridge on Mount Tendurek, twenty-nine kilometres south of Ararat and three from the Iranian border, and a Kurdish shepherd, Reshit Sarihan, sees a boat shape in the ground. It is a hundred and sixty-four metres long, pointed at one end, swelling at the sides. In October 1959 the Turkish army captain Ilhan Durupinar picks the same outline out of aerial photographs taken for NATO mapping, and the formation takes his name.
suggested_refs: The NATO aerial survey photographs of 1959 in which the Durupinar outline was first identified

stops.name: Durupinar, the ground opened and nothing found
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month
stops.campa: In September 1960 an expedition from the Archaeological Research Foundation digs the formation and finds no archaeological remains: no worked timber, no fastenings, no cargo, nothing but soil and rock arranged in the shape of a hull. The report calls it a natural formation, and interest lapses for seventeen years. The ground itself is limonite with magnetite in steeply inclined sedimentary layers, the same beds that fold along the whole ridge, and the boat outline lies where two of those folds happen to meet.
suggested_refs: The 1960 Archaeological Research Foundation report on the Durupinar formation

stops.name: Durupinar, the syncline and the recantation
stops.date_confidence: attested for the 1977 revival; the geological study is 1996 and Fasold's sworn recantation 1997
stops.campa: From 1977 Ron Wyatt promotes the ridge anew as the petrified ark, joined in 1985 by the salvage expert David Fasold and the geophysicist John Baumgardner. In 1996 Fasold co-authors with the geologist Lorence Collins a study concluding that the formation is a doubly plunging syncline, natural to the last grain, and testifying in 1997 Fasold calls the ark claim absolute BS. The young earth creationist geologist Andrew Snelling reaches the same verdict on his own account.
suggested_refs: The 1996 Collins and Fasold paper identifying the Durupinar formation as a doubly plunging syncline

stops.name: Williamstown, the ark rebuilt in Kentucky
stops.date_confidence: attested; the opening date was chosen to echo Genesis 7:7
stops.campa: In Williamstown, Kentucky, a full-size ark opens to the public on the seventh day of the seventh month of 2016, the date chosen for the verse in which the household goes aboard. It is five hundred and ten feet long, eighty-five wide and fifty-one high, some three million three hundred thousand board feet of timber across a hundred and thirty-two bays on three decks, raised by Answers in Genesis to argue that the vessel described in the chapter can be built. It stands seven thousand miles from the mountain.
suggested_refs: The Ark Encounter at Williamstown, Kentucky, opened 7 July 2016
